Opinion 5 - Studies of isolated cells, termed in vitro analyses, help provide information on potential organ-specific effects and the toxicological mechanisms driving health outcomes following exposure to a given compound. In vitro data indicate that kratom alkaloids are primarily metabolized by Cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 and that physiological effects are driven by alkaloid activity at opioid, adrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic receptors. Kratom’s pain relief (analgesic) and euphoric effects can be explained by kratom alkaloid binding at opioid receptors (ORs). However, it is my opinion that the activity of mitragynine, 7-hydroxymitragynine, and other kratom alkaloids at ORs is weak relative to that of numerous drugs (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) and endogenous endorphins (e.g., β-endorphin, enkephalins, dynorphins). However, depending on the dose, 7-hydroxymitragynine can cause morphine like effects if ingested in a relatively pure state (i.e., as a synthetic isolate). Opinion 6 - Data on the effects of kratom use in humans includes epidemiological evidence, as well as information from case reports and case series. It is my opinion that human studies, although limited, indicate that kratom use is associated with potential benefits including stimulant effects, pain relief, and as a substitute or withdrawal aid for opioids at doses yielding few to no adverse behavioral or physiological effects. Case data indicate that kratom’s alkaloids produce few to no acute adverse health effects when kratom is used alone, but that mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine have been reported along with other compounds in the post-mortem blood and tissues of dual- and polysubstance users. Opinion 7 - Based on the records regarding Ms. Moller’s passing, it is likely that she experienced an adverse cardiovascular event, which led to her death. Kratom has not been found to increase the risk of heart attacks in humans. It is my opinion that, should it be determined that Ms. Moller experienced a heart attack or comparable cardiovascular event which resulted in her death, kratom would not have been the cause. 14

BASES FOR OPINIONS Basis of Opinion 1 M. Speciosa Traditional Use 47. Mitragyna speciosa, commonly known as kratom, is a tree native to Southeast Asia, specifically, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Borneo, Myanmar, and Vietnam. M. speciosa can reach up to 25 meters tall at maturity and is noted for having dark green leaves with green, white, or red veins (Cinosi et al. 2015). It conventionally grows in swampy areas, in areas inundated by water, and alongside riverbanks (Grundmann 2017; Ahmad et al. 2022). Depending on the country, kratom is referred to by its local name: ketum or biak (Malaysia), keton or kadamba (Indonesia), benisa (Myanmar), mambog or lugub (Philippines), ithang, thom, kratom (Thailand), or giam (Vietnam) (Gong et al. 2012; Cinosi et al. 2015; Grundmann 2017; Eastlack et al. 2020). 48. Kratom leaves were historically used in rural communities by farmers, laborers, or fishermen in Southeast Asia as a stimulant to reduce or prevent fatigue stemming from hard labor by chewing the leaves raw or drying them for later consumption (Cinosi et al. 2015; Grundmann 2017; Singh et al. 2017). Although less common in Southeast Asia, it is reported that the dried 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 19 of 429 leaves of kratom can also be smoked to achieve a relaxing effect (Grundmann 2017). Medicinally, kratom was traditionally used to treat symptoms of substance abuse disorders (including opium withdrawal), headaches, toothaches, diarrhea, cough, fever, stroke symptoms, sleeplessness, typhoid, cholesterol issues, stimulate appetite, pain, cough, hypertension, diabetes, anxiety, as a wound poultice, and as a deworming agent (Gong et al. 2012; Grundmann 2017; Eastlack et al. 2020; Ahmad et al. 2022). Very few of these benefits have been studied in clinical settings. 49. Apart from medicinal uses, Kratom was also utilized for centuries for social purposes and to perform cultural and religious ceremonies in Southeast Asia (Cinosi et al. 2015; Singh et al. 2017). It was reported that kratom was used as a substitute for alcohol in predominately Muslim communities in Malaysia and South Thailand (Singh et al. 2017; Charoenratana et al. 2021). In Thailand, kratom has been recognized as a culturally significant plant as of the 19th century (Charoenratana et al. 2021). 50. Plants in the genus, Mitragyna, that are native to Africa, historically were used to treat various disease, such as malaria, rheumatism, cardiovascular disease, amenorrhea, inflammation, headaches, bronchopulmonary disease, and diabetes mellitus (Ahmad et al. 2022). The first description of kratom as Mitragyna by a western scientist came from Dutch botanist Pieter Willem Korthals, who travelled through Southeast Asia with the Dutch East India Company Commission for Natural Science from 1830 to 1837 (Ahmad et al. 2022). Mr. Korthal eponymously described the now commercially significant cultivar of kratom, Mitragyna speciosa Korth, though several other species are also classified within the genus. M. In Southeast Asia, people consume kratom by smoking or chewing the plant’s leaves and via brewing a tea to drink (Singh et al. 2016). Potential Adverse Effects 71. When data on the toxicity of kratom and its alkaloids is viewed relative to historic toxicological classifications, it can be classified as moderately toxic (Hodge and Sterner 1949). However, when animal data are considered, traditional kratom preparations (e.g., teas, leaves) represent a low acute or repeated dose toxicity profile. Animal studies have consistently determined that there are little or no chronic adverse effects expected from kratom use at typical doses, and animals exposed to high levels of kratom recover quickly after exposure ceased. It should be noted that kratom and mitragynine have been cited as factors in several studies of overdose deaths across the U.S. (Olsen et al. 2019). However, these results are confounded in that nearly all users had taken other substances as well. 72. Both the National Institute of Drug Abuse (NIDA) and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) have noted the addictive potential and prevalence of withdrawal symptoms following kratom use but recognized the reduced addictive potential and mild withdrawal symptoms relative to opioids (Commission on Narcotic Drugs 2021; National Institute on Drug Abuse 2023). Basis of Opinion 2 Introduction to the Risk Assessment Process 76. The risk assessment process is a methodology that is widely accepted and used by many scientific bodies and governmental agencies around the world. It is an appropriate method to use for characterizing the health risks potentially associated with use of kratom products (especially when comparing potential health risks associated with kratom use to those associated with use of opioids to yield similar effects). 77. Over the past 50 years, risk assessments have received widespread attention and acceptance within the scientific and regulatory communities (Starr 1969; National Research Council (NRC) 1983; Commission on Risk Assessment 1997). In its 1983 report, the National Academy of Sciences defined “risk assessment” as: “[C]haracterization of the potential adverse health effects of human exposures to environmental hazards. Risk assessments include several elements: description of the potential adverse health effects based on an evaluation of results of epidemiologic, clinical, toxicologic, and environmental research; extrapolation from those results to predict the type and estimate the extent of health effects in humans under given conditions of exposure; judgements as to the number and characteristics of persons exposed at various intensities and durations; and summary judgements of the existence and overall magnitude of the public-health problem. Risk assessment also includes characterization of the uncertainties inherent in the process of inferring risk” (National Research Council (NRC) 1983). 78. The endorsement of the risk assessment methodology is discussed in the three documents issued by the National Academies of Sciences over the past 40 years (National Research Council (NRC) 1983, 1994, 2009). 25

Risk assessment comprises four major steps: hazard identification, dose-response assessment, exposure assessment, and risk characterization (National Research Council (NRC) 1983). 80. Hazard identification is the most recognized of the actions of regulatory agencies. It is defined here as the process of determining if human exposure to an agent could cause an increase in the incidence of a health condition (e.g., cancer, birth defect), or if a nonhuman receptor (e.g., fish, birds, other wildlife) might be adversely affected following exposure. It involves characterizing the nature and strength of the evidence of causation. Although the question of whether a substance causes cancer or other adverse health effects in humans is theoretically a yes- no question, there are few chemicals or physical agents with definitive human data (National Research Council (NRC) 1983). Therefore, the question is often restated in terms of effects in laboratory animals or other test systems: Does the agent induce cancer in test animals? Positive answers to such questions are typically taken as evidence that an agent may pose a cancer risk for an exposed human. Information from short-term in vitro tests and structural similarity to known chemical hazards may, in certain circumstances, be considered adequate information for hazard identification. 81. Dose-response assessment is the process of characterizing the relationship between the dose of an agent administered or received and the incidence of an adverse health effect as a function of exposure to the agent. This process considers factors such as intensity of exposure and age pattern of exposure, along with variables that might affect response such as sex, lifestyle, and other modifying factors. A dose-response assessment usually requires extrapolation from high to low doses, from animals to humans, and from laboratory animal species to wildlife species. A dose-response assessment should describe and justify the methods of extrapolation used to predict incidence, and it should characterize the statistical and biologic uncertainties in these methods. 82. Exposure assessment is the process of measuring or estimating the intensity, frequency, and duration of human or animal exposure to an agent currently present in the environment, or of estimating hypothetical exposures that might arise from the release of new 26

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 30 of 429 chemicals into the environment. In its most complete form, an exposure assessment should describe the magnitude, duration, schedule, and route of exposure; the size, nature, and classes of the human, animal, aquatic, or wildlife populations exposed; and the uncertainties in all estimates. An exposure assessment can often be used to identify prospective control options and to predict the effects of available control technologies on exposure control. 83. Risk characterization is the process of estimating the incidence of a health effect under various conditions of human or animal exposure described in the exposure assessment. It is performed by combining the exposure and dose-response assessments. The summary effects of the uncertainties in the preceding steps should be described in this step (National Research Council (NRC) 1983). 84. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 31 of 429 85. The Federal government has used the risk assessment process since as early as the 1950s. The FDA commissioner at the time, Arnold Lehman, wrote the first guidelines on how to make decisions when evaluating the safety of drugs, which later became known as the risk assessment process (Paustenbach et al. 1990). 86. Between the 1950s and 1970s, risk assessments were conducted by various government agencies but were often not identified as “risk assessments.” The process was codified in 1983 by the National Academy of Sciences in what has been called “the Red book” (e.g., Risk Assessment in the Federal Government). Since then, risk assessment has been used by virtually every government agency in the United States and by various entities abroad. The general guidance has been routinely updated. 87. Agencies including OSHA, FDA, and CPSC use the risk assessment process any time there is concern about a chemical or radionuclide in any media including food, air, water, sediments, pharmaceutical agents, agricultural agents, medical implants, cosmetics, and consumer products, among other applications. It is essentially the foundation for regulating or characterizing the risk posed by virtually any product made from chemicals. Experience Designing Risk Assessments 88. Basis of Opinion 3 The Health Effects of Kratom Can Be Attributed to More Than 50 Indole Alkaloids 95. The health effects of kratom can be attributed to more than 50 indole alkaloids present in the plant. Of these, mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine are the most biologically significant. It is my opinion that alkaloid concentrations vary across kratom product types, but data from the peer-reviewed literature indicates that these typical concentrations contained in teas or capsules, taken in a reasonable manner, would not increase the risk of acute or chronic adverse health effects among typical users. 96. The health effects of kratom are primarily attributed to its diverse array of alkaloids, with mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine being the most prominent (Grundmann 2017; Singh et al. 2017; Eastlack et al. 2020). These alkaloids interact with opioid receptors in the brain, which can produce pain-relieving, euphoric, and sedative effects. 97. A study conducted by Garcia-Romeu et al. (2020) describes kratom use patterns among regular users in the United States, for both medicinal and recreational consumption. The majority of respondents reported moderate dosing, with 49.0% consuming 1–3 grams per dose and 33.4% consuming 4–6 grams across product types, which the study design and convenience sample did not distinguish. Smaller groups reported using less than 1 gram (8.6%) and more than 7 grams (8.9%) per dose. The study also revealed high frequency of use, with 59.1% of participants using kratom daily, 18.2% of participants using kratom 4-6 times per week, and 13.4% of participants using kratom 2-3 times per week. The preferred methods of consumption were as a prepared beverage (37.0%), ingested as raw powder (43.6%), and in capsule form (18.9%). The authors reported that this varied consumption underscores the integration of kratom into daily routines to potentially manage pain or as an alternative to opioids. The modes of consumption influence the pharmacokinetics of kratom's alkaloids, affecting both therapeutic outcomes and the potential for 30

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 34 of 429 adverse effects, highlighting the need for careful consideration of kratom's use, regulatory oversight, and further research to understand its full implications and mitigate associated risks (Garcia-Romeu et al. 2020). Kratom Dosing 98. The dosing of kratom for humans varies significantly based on its intended effects, which range from stimulation to sedation. Low doses of approximately 1-5 grams of kratom leaves are considered stimulating, similar to the effect of drinking coffee, providing increased alertness and physical energy (Warner et al. 2016). Medium doses ranging from 5 to 15 grams produce more opioid-like effects, such as pain relief and euphoria, but can also cause side effects such as dizziness and nausea. High doses exceeding 15 grams tend to produce sedation and can cause severe side effects, including stupor and potentially toxic effects (Warner et al. 2016). 99. Online websites usually advertise kratom as a legal substitute for opioids and other substances, claiming various therapeutic benefits. According to an online post, “Kratom dosage recommendations typically range from 2 to 12 grams, with doses under 2 grams considered microdoses and doses over 6 grams considered high doses” (Moore 2024b). The website reported that the self-treatment of depression symptoms could be treated with kratom doses between 2 and 6 grams while doses for mild to moderate chronic pain were between 4 and 8 grams. The recommended dosage for opioid withdrawal was between 2 and 12 grams, for anxiety was up to 6 grams, and for energy and focus was between 2 and 4 grams (Moore 2024b) Kratom Alkaloids Mitragynine 100. Mitragynine is the most abundant alkaloid in kratom, accounting for approximately 60-70% of the alkaloid content of most such plants. It acts on the mu-opioid receptors (µORs) as a partial agonist (Prozialeck et al. 2012). This interaction is responsible for the analgesic properties of kratom but with a reportedly lower risk of respiratory depression compared to opioids (Prozialeck et al. 2012). The mechanism underlying this is discussed later in my report. However, mitragynine also interacts with other receptor systems, including adrenergic, serotonergic, and 31

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 35 of 429 dopaminergic pathways, which can contribute to both its therapeutic effects and potential adverse side effects (Prozialeck et al. 2012). Mitragynine is the most significant kratom alkaloid with respect to pharmacological and toxicological evaluations, largely due to its abundance in the plants. 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) 101. Though present in much smaller amounts (up to 2% of total plant alkaloid content), 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) is significantly more potent than mitragynine with respect to pharmacological and toxicological potential (Sharma and McCurdy 2021). Specifically, 7-HMG is about 13 to 46 times more potent than mitragynine, primarily because of the addition of a hydroxyl group at the C7 position on the indole ring (Prozialeck et al. 2012). This modification increases its binding affinity and efficacy at µORs, which are primarily responsible for kratom’s analgesic (pain-relieving, or anti-nociceptive) effects (Obeng et al. 2020). The presence of this hydroxyl group facilitates better interactions with the receptor, enhancing kratom’s opioid receptor agonist properties (Obeng et al. 2020; Obeng et al. 2021). 102. Biologically, 7-HMG induces pain relief responses in a dose-dependent manner, acting predominantly as a full agonist at µORs, which differentiates its effects from those of mitragynine, which acts as only a partial agonist (Obeng et al. 2021). Despite its relatively low concentrations in kratom products, 7-HMG’s pharmacological profile suggests significant implications for pain management, while also raising concerns regarding its abuse potential due to the potent and efficacious opioid receptor activation (Kruegel et al. 2019). Further, as a metabolite of mitragynine, the effects of 7-HMG are modulated not only by direct intake from kratom products (which is quite low), but also formation from mitragynine within the body (Kruegel et al. 2019). Speciociliatine is a weak opioid receptor antagonist, bearing a structural similarity to mitragynine (Prozialeck et al. 2012). As a weak antagonist, it potentially mitigates some of the effects of mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, thereby possibly reducing the risk of dependence and abuse associated with kratom (Prozialeck et al. 2012). According to Kamble et al. (2021), speciociliatine more potently stimulates μOR-mediated G protein-coupled signaling in vitro than mitragynine. 108. Some in vivo studies have demonstrated that speciociliatine can act as an opioid agonist. For example, it has been shown to produce antinociceptive effects in animal models, which are indicative of opioid-like activity (Hanapi et al. 2021). In contrast, certain in vitro studies reported that speciociliatine exhibited weak antagonistic activity at opioid receptors; some cellular models determined that speciociliatine could block or dampen the receptor activity typically stimulated by other potent agonists like mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (Takayama et al. 2002; Kruegel et al. 2016). This suggests that the stereochemistry at the C-3 position of the speciociliatine molecule could be crucial in enhancing its binding affinity and subsequent pharmacological response (Karunakaran et al. 2022). Speciogynine 109. Known for its role as a smooth muscle relaxer, speciogynine is an important alkaloid in terms of the therapeutic applications of kratom (Prozialeck et al. 2012). By contributing 37

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 41 of 429 muscle relaxant properties, it can enhance the therapeutic potential of kratom for users seeking relief from physical discomfort without psychoactive effects (Hanapi et al. 2021). Paynantheine 110. Paynantheine is considered the second most abundant alkaloid in some kratom extracts, accounting for about 10% of the total alkaloid content (World Health Organization (WHO) 2021). While paynantheine is known for its muscle relaxant properties, it does not primarily act through opioid receptor pathways like some of the other kratom alkaloids. Instead, its mode of action is more associated with mechanisms similar to those of other muscle relaxants, which may involve modulation of calcium influx or influence on other non-opioid receptor pathways (Takayama 2004). Corynantheidine 111. Corynantheidine is an opioid antagonist at µORs, essentially blocking the receptor and preventing the typical opioid effects such as pain relief, which would otherwise be mediated by agonists like 7-hydroxymitragynine or morphine. In kratom, corynantheidine’s opioid antagonistic properties may serve to balance the effects of opioid agonists, potentially reducing the addictive qualities and other negative side effects associated with opioid-like compounds (Hanapi et al. 2021). Vape shops and online vendors often provide a range of kratom products, catering to both novice and experienced kratom users. The availability of such a wide array of kratom products online and in vape shops highlights the substance’s growing popularity as both a recreational substance and a self-medication method (Prozialeck et al. 2012; Henningfield et al. 2018). 38

Leaves 113. Traditionally, fresh or dried kratom leaves from the M. speciosa are chewed or made into tea; they are seldom smoked (European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction 2015). Kratom leaves are distinguished by the color of the veins running through them, which can be white, green, or red. This color variation is commonly used in the marketing and classification of kratom in Western countries, where the leaves are primarily sold as powdered extracts. 40

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 44 of 429 114. Each vein color is often associated with different effects, which are attributed to variations in the chemical composition and concentration of alkaloids within the leaves (Veltri and Grundmann 2019). Chewing the fresh leaves of kratom releases alkaloids such as mitragynine into the bloodstream more directly. This practice is common among laborers in countries like Thailand and Malaysia, where kratom is used to reduce muscle pain and enhance productivity during long hours of physical labor (Veltri and Grundmann 2019). 115. The alkaloid content in kratom leaves, particularly mitragynine and 7- hydroxymitragynine, varies significantly depending on factors like the plant's geographic origin and the methods used in its processing. Dry kratom leaves typically contain about 0.5% to 1.5% alkaloids by weight (Hassan et al. 2013). Mitragynine is the predominant alkaloid, comprising over 60% of the total alkaloid content, while 7-hydroxymitragynine accounts for about 2% (Lydecker et al. 2016; Kruegel and Grundmann 2018). Other minor alkaloids such as speciociliatine, speciogynine, and paynantheine contribute 9%, 7%, and 10%, respectively, to the total alkaloid profile (Takayama 2004; Kruegel and Grundmann 2018). The concentration of these alkaloids can vary widely in commercially available kratom products in the U.S., ranging from 0.7% to 38.74% for mitragynine and 0.01% to 0.75% for 7-hydroxymitragynine in products like capsules, dried leaves, powders, resins, and concentrated extracts (Kikura-Hanajiri et al. 2009; Sharma et al. 2019). 116. Kratom grown in the United States has been identified as having a distinct chemotype, richer in oxindole alkaloids compared to its counterparts in Asia and Africa (Raffa 2014). In young Thai kratom plants, speciogynine is the dominant alkaloid found in the leaves, whereas in the fruits of Malaysian kratom plants, speciociliatine is more prevalent (Kitajima et al. 2005; Raffa 2014). Wet Leaves 117. Fresh, wet kratom leaves contain all the plant's natural alkaloids in their original concentrations. When kratom is freshly harvested, the alkaloids are present in their most natural state (Zhang et al. 2020). However, the total alkaloid content in fresh leaves is generally lower by 41

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 45 of 429 weight compared to dry leaves, primarily because fresh leaves contain a significant amount of water. When kratom leaves are fresh, the alkaloids are naturally protected within the plant’s cell structure. Chewing fresh leaves can release these alkaloids effectively, though the bioavailability might be different compared to dried and powdered forms where cell walls have been broken down, potentially making alkaloids more readily available upon ingestion (Hassan et al. 2013; Zhang et al. 2022). Dry Leaves 118. Drying kratom leaves is a common method for preserving them and concentrating their alkaloids. As the water content in the leaves evaporates, the alkaloids become more concentrated by weight. Therefore, dry leaves typically have a higher alkaloid content than fresh leaves (Zhang et al. 2022). Drying methods can affect the alkaloid profile; for example, drying leaves in the sun can degrade certain alkaloids, while shade drying might preserve them better (Zhang et al. 2022). A study by Zhang et al. (2022) quantified nine different kratom alkaloids and found that mitragynine, paynantheine, and corynoxine concentrations were significantly higher in leaves from shaded environments. This indicated that lower light intensities may enhance the synthesis of certain key alkaloids, which are important for kratom's psychoactive and medicinal properties (Zhang et al. 2022). 119. Other studies have shown that alkaloids such as paynantheine, speciogynine, mitraphylline, speciociliatine, and corynantheidine had concentrations ranging from 0.1% to 12.8% by weight in dry leaf powder or extracts (Hassan et al. 2013; Cinosi et al. 2015; Montserrat- de la Paz et al. 2015; Obeng et al. 2020). The stability of certain alkaloids during drying can vary, with some being more susceptible to degradation due to environmental factors such as light, temperature, and humidity. The dried leaves can then be used in various forms, such as powder, which is commonly used for making tea or capsules. Seasonal and Geographic Differences in Alkaloid Concentrations 120. M. speciosa from Thailand has higher mitragynine content than M. speciosa from Malaysia (Takayama et al. 1998). Specifically, looking at Thailand, a study by Leksungnoen et al. 42

Four regions in Thailand, north, northeast, central, and south, were also investigated and found to influence the metabolic profile of the plant; mitragynine content ranged from 7.5 to 26.6 mg per gram of dry leaf weight across all regions, with an average of 16.0 ± 5.7 mg per gram (Leksungnoen et al. 2022). 121. The highest mitragynine concentrations of 18.5 to 21.8 mg per gram of dry leaf weight were generally found in samples from the central and southern regions of Thailand (Leksungnoen et al. 2022). This was further qualified when the lowest concentrations (approximately 11.4 mg per gram of dry leaf weight) were found in the northern and northeastern regions of Thailand, which generally have lower light intensity and different soil characteristics (Leksungnoen et al. 2022). 122. Application of fertilizer significantly increased plant growth metrics such as height, width, trunk size, leaf number and area, and total dry mass (Zhang et al. 2020, 2022). This suggested that kratom responded well to nutrient supplementation, enhancing overall biomass without signs of nitrogen toxicity, even at high application rates. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 47 of 429 123. Brewed tea is a traditional and still commonly used method of kratom consumption in the United States and elsewhere. Kratom powder, kratom extract, or the dried leaves (loose or in a tea bag) are steeped in hot water, which extracts the alkaloids into the liquid. Background on Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics 137. Pharmacokinetic studies describe the way mammals process, that is, absorb, metabolize, distribute, and eliminate compounds to which they are exposed. Pharmacodynamic and toxicodynamic studies refer to the study of the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs on the body, as well as the mechanisms by which these effects are produced. Such studies indicate 47

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 51 of 429 that kratom’s physiological effects occur within minutes of product use and generally peak within one to four hours of use, depending on dose. It is my opinion that based on the elimination half- life data for mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine in humans, kratom associated alkaloids are generally eliminated (or greater than 95% eliminated) from the human body within two to 24 hours of product use, depending on dose and use frequency. 138. Pharmacokinetic studies describe the ways that organisms biologically process compounds to which they are exposed intentionally, such as via drug administration, or unintentionally, such as via secondhand or environmental exposures. These are often termed studies of the time course of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME). In contrast, pharmacodynamic studies describe the physiological effects of a compound on the body. 139. As noted previously, kratom is consumed in various forms such as chewing leaves, drinking teas and juices, via capsules, powdered in iced cocktails, or via smoking, though the latter is uncommon due to the high volume of leaves needed and their high cellulose content, which makes smoking less effective (Tanguay and International Drug Policy Consortium 2011; Hassan et al. 2013; Brown et al. 2017; Henningfield et al. 2018; Veltri and Grundmann 2019; Braley and Hondrogiannis 2020; Eastlack et al. 2020). The potency of kratom varies with the strain and age of the plant; older, green-veined leaves are typically more potent than younger, red-veined ones, and users should consider these differences when selecting products (Brown et al. 2017; Veltri and Grundmann 2019; Braley and Hondrogiannis 2020; Swogger et al. 2022). Pharmacokinetics 140. Following consumption, mitragynine is absorbed rapidly due to its high lipid solubility and ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. The elimination of mitragynine from the body follows a biphasic pattern, initially distributing quickly then diminishing more slowly indicates that while the plant’s physiological effects may start quickly, they could also last several hours, depending on the dose. The primary metabolic processing occurs in the liver via cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes, producing various metabolites that may influence both its therapeutic 48

In contrast, 7-hydroxymitragynine, though less abundant in kratom, is more potent and metabolized similarly to mitragynine. Pharmacodynamics 141. Mitragynine’s interaction with opioid receptors, particularly µORs and δORs where it acts as a partial agonist, underlies the analgesic and mildly euphoric effects observed at lower doses. Though found in smaller amounts, 7-hydroxymitragynine is a stronger µOR agonist, enhancing its pain-relieving efficacy. Beyond ORs, these alkaloids also modulate other neurotransmitter systems such as the adrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic pathways, affecting mood and pain perception. Their ability to engage these receptors without the full receptor activation seen with traditional opioids suggests they might offer pain relief with potentially lower risks of dependency and fewer side effects (such as a reduced risk of respiratory depression). 142. The differing effects and potencies across kratom alkaloids render such products multifaceted pharmacological substances with stimulant or sedative outcomes based on dose and the proportion of mitragynine to 7-hydroxymitragynine. The pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties provide a foundation for understanding how mitragynine and 7- hydroxymitragynine might be used therapeutically, the risks associated with their use, and the strategies for mitigating these risks. This information is essential for healthcare providers, researchers, and policymakers in determining the safe and effective use of kratom and its constituents in clinical settings or regulating their use in consumer products. The pharmacokinetics of individual alkaloids cannot always predict the pharmacology of the overall mixture of alkaloids in kratom products due to the presence of multiple compounds at different concentrations, which could influence each compounds pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. 171. Comparison to Pharmacokinetics of other Botanical and Medicinal Products 186. Theobromine, caffeine, yohimbine, and kratom (mitragynine) are naturally derived alkaloids with psychoactive properties that affect the central nervous system. Caffeine is found in coffee beans, tea leaves, and cocoa beans; theobromine is primarily found in cocoa beans and chocolate; yohimbine is extracted from the bark of the Yohimbe tree; kratom is derived from the leaves of the M. speciosa tree. They interact with specific receptors or enzymes to influence physiological and psychological states, varying from stimulation to sedation. Commonly used both medicinally and recreationally, these compounds enhance alertness, mood, and physical performance, although they differ in their primary effects and mechanisms of action. Each demonstrates a capability to be utilized in managing fatigue and altering mood, making them significant in both therapeutic settings and everyday use. Their natural alkaloid classification highlights a shared chemical characteristic that contributes to their bioactive profiles. 187. Pharmacokinetic properties associated with 7-hydroxymitragynine are generally considered to be similar with mitragynine. The compounds display some similarity and differences in their pharmacokinetic properties. Absorption 188. The pharmacokinetic absorption profiles of theobromine, caffeine, yohimbine, and kratom (mitragynine) have similar rates of uptake from the gastrointestinal tract. Theobromine is 64

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 68 of 429 absorbed more slowly, reaching peak plasma levels around 2-3 hours after ingestion, whereas caffeine is absorbed most rapidly, achieving peak concentrations within 15-45 minutes. Yohimbine and kratom are absorbed relatively quickly as well, with peak plasma levels typically reached within about one hour for yohimbine and approximately 1.5 hours for kratom (Mumford et al. 1996). Distribution 189. These compounds are distributed throughout the body, though the extent to which they cross the blood-brain barrier, their affinity for specific tissues, and their volume of distribution vary. Theobromine is widely distributed through all body fluids with a larger volume of distribution than caffeine, indicating extensive tissue reach. Caffeine, known for its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier easily, is well-distributed throughout the body, including the brain, enhancing its stimulatory effects on the central nervous system. Yohimbine, like caffeine, crosses the blood-brain barrier and shows a high affinity for both fat tissues and the central nervous system, suggesting a targeted therapeutic action on these areas. Mitragynine is characterized by its high plasma protein binding and extensive distribution, which may influence its duration of action and efficacy in pain relief (Arnaud 1988, 2011). Metabolism 190. The metabolism of theobromine, caffeine, yohimbine, and kratom's primary active component mitragynine occurs primarily in the liver, involving the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, albeit involving different specific enzymes (e.g., CYP1A2 for caffeine, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 for mitragynine). This shows that the compounds share a common metabolic pathway but varied specifics in metabolic processing (Owen et al. 1987; Philipp et al. 2011a; Philipp et al. 2011b). The engagement of the cytochrome P450 system in their metabolism suggests potential interactions with other compounds metabolized by this system, affecting efficacy and safety profiles. Excretion 65

Conclusions on Kratom Pharmacokinetics 192. The pharmacokinetics of kratom, particularly its primary alkaloids mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, reveal a complex interaction within the human body that is influenced by various factors including dose, frequency of use, and the form of kratom preparation. Studies have shown that these alkaloids are rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, with peak concentrations typically reached within hours of ingestion. Mitragynine exhibits a biphasic elimination pattern with a terminal half-life suggesting rapid metabolism and minimal potential for accumulation in tissues with typical use patterns. The pharmacokinetics of kratom are further complicated by the presence of multiple compounds in the plant, which can affect each compound’s absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. This complexity is underscored by findings that commercial kratom products can lead to higher systemic exposure and delayed absorption compared to traditional preparations. 193. The pharmacodynamics of mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, as partial agonists of the human µ-opioid receptor (µOR), suggest potential therapeutic applications, particularly in pain management, while also highlighting the risks of adverse interactions with drugs metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes. The high plasma protein binding of 7- hydroxymitragynine indicates a prolonged presence in the bloodstream, which, coupled with its rapid metabolism, suggested a complex excretion pattern likely involving metabolites. However, these alkaloids are partial agonists at the human µOR, showing functional selectivity for G-protein signaling without significantly recruiting β-arrestin, which is associated with the adverse effects of traditional opioids. This selective binding potentially contributes to fewer side effects, making 66

Basis of Opinion 4 The Importance of In Vivo Studies of Kratom 194. Human data is the gold standard when evaluating the toxicological and pharmacological effects of a compound. Specifically, controlled clinical studies that include an array of doses can help provide information about a compound’s beneficial and adverse effects. For kratom, several previously detailed pharmacokinetic studies clarified how mitragynine and 7- hydroxymitragynine are absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted from the human body (Trakulsrichai et al. 2015; Tanna et al. 2022; Huestis et al. 2024). However, these studies, while informative, provided minimal insight into the beneficial or adverse effects of kratom alkaloids at specific doses. That is, it can be concluded from the pharmacokinetic analyses that tested doses (which at times exceeded 50 mg/kg-bw mitragynine) did not yield overt signs of human toxicity, but they by design did not establish doses at which specific health effects occurred. Similarly, the epidemiological and case report/series data for kratom, which I discuss later in my report, cannot be used to determine dose-specific alkaloid effects. 195. The above limitations of human pharmacokinetic, epidemiological, and case report/series inquiries highlight the importance of in vivo data. No animal studies present a perfect model of potential human outcomes. Yet in vivo methods can help inform toxicological conclusions and risk assessments in the absence of robust human data on adverse effect levels, which is the case for kratom. Moreover, such studies can be more easily extrapolated to human effects than in vitro tests even though the latter methods have provided valuable insight into the mechanisms driving kratom’s physiological activity. 196. The in vivo data on kratom and its alkaloids has yet to fully resolve whole body or organ/tissue-specific dose effects across a broad suite of routes and frequency of administration (i.e., no-observed-adverse-effect-levels (NOAELs) and lowest-observed-adverse-effect-levels (LOAELs) need to be better established). Nonetheless, the information generally indicates that 67

As discussed above, kratom and its alkaloids show beneficial effects, foremost pain relief (analgesia) and stimulant outcomes, at doses experienced by typical kratom users. Based on the methods of Hodge and Sterner (1949), this indicates that kratom is generally “slightly” to “moderately” acutely toxic, with the greatest concern associated with 7- hydroxymitragynine (which represents a very small component of the alkaloid content of most products). Studies of isolated cells, termed in vitro analyses, help provide information on potential organ-specific effects and the toxicological mechanisms driving health outcomes following exposure to a given compound. In vitro data indicate that kratom alkaloids are primarily metabolized by Cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 and that physiological effects are driven by alkaloid activity at opioid, adrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic receptors. Kratom’s pain relief (analgesic) and euphoric effects can be explained by kratom alkaloid binding at opioid receptors (ORs). However, it is my opinion that the activity of mitragynine, 7-hydroxymitragynine, and other kratom alkaloids at ORs is weak relative to that of numerous drugs (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) and endogenous endorphins (e.g., β-endorphin, enkephalins, dynorphins). The estimated doses for all consumption types ranged from 0.015 to 158 mg/kg- bw/day, where the highest dose was achieved through the consumption of kratom tea. The lowest lethal dose observed in single- and repeated-dose in vivo studies in mice using subcutaneous, intraperitoneal, and oral routes of administration ranged from 200 to 1,098 mg/kg-bw (Grewal 1932b; Macko et al. 1972; Sabetghadam et al. 2013a; Singh et al. 2019; Chakraborty et al. 2021). 450. Taking a conservative approach by applying the lowest observed lethal dose (200 mg/kg-bw), the estimated doses are between 1.27- and 13,333-fold lower than expected lethal doses. If the upper estimate of observed lethal dose is considered, the estimated values are between 6.95- and 73,200-fold lower than expected lethal doses. Specific to the oral route of administration, which is the most relevant, these estimates are approximately 3- to 50,000-fold below the LD50 values for mitragynine in vivo. 451. Our estimates (0.015 to 158 mg/kg-bw/day) generally fell within the range of mitragynine doses reported to yield few to no adverse effects in single- and repeated-dose in vivo studies in mice, rats, and dogs (Macko et al. 1972; Sabetghadam et al. 2013a; Sabetghadam et al. 2013b). Macko et al. (1972) reported few to no adverse effects following oral administration of mitragynine at 5 to 50 mg/kg-bw/day, and Sabetghadam et al. (2013b) reported no overt signs of oral toxicity at 1, 10, and 100 mg/kg-bw/day, apart from piloerection and increased liver weight at 10 and 100 mg/kg-bw/day. This indicates that some margin of safety should be present between mitragynine concentrations ingested by the majority of United States kratom consumers and mitragynine concentrations expected to yield adverse effects with acute or chronic use. While it is unknown how much kratom Ms. Moller ingested in the day or days prior to her passing, typical kratom doses would not result in adverse health effects, including cardiovascular health effects. 161
